## The Setting (At Least, Initially)

- The one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) model is
\begin{eqnarray*}
Y_{ij} = \mu + \tau_i + \epsilon_{ij}
\end{eqnarray*}

  + $\mu$: an overall mean response value (a constant)

  + $\tau_i$: a deterministic shift in the mean for group $i$ (also constant)

  + $\epsilon_{ij}$: the random variation for datum $j$ of group $i$

  + $Y_{ij}$: the observed value for datum $j$ of group $i$

- Within this model, there is an implicit assumption that every possible group has been identified and is represented in the dataset

  + for instance, in a particular study, we might have vaccine-taking, placebo-taking, and no treatment groups, and these would be the only three possible groups

- What if, for instance, we only have data for some subset of all possible groups?

  + for instance, in a particular study, we might examine data for all the players on $m$ teams in a league, where the overall number of teams is $n > m$

  + the answer: we should move to the setting of *random effects modeling*


---

## The Setting (At Least, Initially)

- For the setting in which we are analyzing groups of data (first, without regard to any possible predictor variables), the corresponding random effects model will be
\begin{eqnarray*}
Y_{ij} = \mu + \tau_i + \epsilon_{ij}
\end{eqnarray*}

  + "uh...this is the same model as on the last slide"
  
  + well, yes, but actually no: the ANOVA model assumes the $\tau_i$'s are constants, whereas here we're assuming that $\tau_i \sim {\rm N}(0,\,\sigma_\tau^2)$
  
  + *note*: in both models, we have the same assumption on $\epsilon_{ij} \sim {\rm N}(0,\,\sigma^2)$
  
- "But how does this change the model, really?"

- Well, one-way ANOVA modeling and random effects modeling have different goals:

  + one-way ANOVA: perform the hypothesis test $\mathcal{H}_0: \tau_1 = \cdots = \tau_k$ versus $\mathcal{H}_A:$ "at least one of the $\tau_i$'s differs from the others"
  
  + random effects modelling: quantify how large $\sigma_\tau^2$ (the variance of the means across groups) is compared to $\sigma^2$ (the variance of the data within each group)
  
- For a still somewhat high-level, but slightly deeper introduction, you might take a look at [this presentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/education/semesters/as2015/anova/06_Random_Effects.pdf)


---

## Example: Calf Birth Weight

.pull-left[

<br><br><br><br><br>

- The data shown at right come from [this book](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~meier/teaching/anova/random-and-mixed-effects-models.html)

  + they show the birth weight of calves born to five different fathers ("sires")
  
  + since the number of possible sires is $\gg 5$, a random effects model is appropriate here

]

.pull-right[
```{r echo=FALSE,fig.align="center",fig.width=6,fig.height=6}
# https://people.math.ethz.ch/~meier/teaching/anova/random-and-mixed-effects-models.html
#  First let's create data set
weight <- c(61, 100,  56, 113,  99, 103,  75,  62,   ## sire 1
            75, 102,  95, 103,  98, 115,  98,  94,   ## sire 2
            58,  60,  60,  57,  57,  59,  54, 100,   ## sire 3
            57,  56,  67,  59,  58, 121, 101, 101,   ## sire 4
            59,  46, 120, 115, 115,  93, 105,  75)   ## sire 5
sire    <- factor(rep(1:5, each = 8))
animals <- data.frame(weight, sire)
suppressMessages(library(tidyverse))
ggplot(data = animals, mapping = aes(x = sire, y = weight)) +
  geom_point(col = "seagreen") + xlab("Sire") + ylab("Weight")
```
]

## Example: Calf Birth Weight

.pull-left[

```{r eval=FALSE}
# this package needs to be installed!
suppressMessages(library(lme4))

# 1 | sire <-> "a random intercept for each sire"
#  (more on this notation later)
re.out <- lmer(weight ~ 1 | sire, data = animals)
summary(re.out)
```

- REML = "restricted maximum likelihood"

  + a maximum likelihood estimator that aims to counteract biases in the estimation of variances
  
- Fixed effect: the mean birth weight is 82.55

- Random effects: 

  + the sire-to-sire variance in birth weight is estimated to be $\sigma_\tau^2 = 116.7$ (so that the standard deviation is $\sqrt{116.7} = 10.81$)

  + the within-sire variance in birth weight is $\sigma^2 = 463.8$ (standard deviation $\sqrt{463.8} = 21.54$)
]

.pull-right[
```{r echo=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
# this package needs to be installed!
suppressMessages(library(lme4))

# a random intercept for each sire
#  (more on this notation later)
re.out <- lmer(weight ~ 1 | sire, data = animals)   
summary(re.out)
```
]


---

## Example: Calf Birth Weight

.pull-left[

```{r eval=FALSE}
# this package needs to be installed!
suppressMessages(library(lme4))

# 1 | sire <-> "a random intercept for each sire"
#  (more on this notation later)
re.out <- lmer(weight ~ 1 | sire, data = animals)
summary(re.out)
```

- The overall variance in birth weights is $\sigma^2 + \sigma_\tau^2 = 580.5$

- The correlation (a quantification of the magnitude of linear dependence) between two calves of:

  + different sires: 0 (no correlation; by assumption)
  
  + the same sire: $\sigma_\tau^2/(\sigma_\tau^2+\sigma^2) = 0.20$ (this would generally be considered a "weak" correlation)

]

.pull-right[
```{r echo=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
# this package needs to be installed!
suppressMessages(library(lme4))

# a random intercept for each sire
#  (more on this notation later)
re.out <- lmer(weight ~ 1 | sire, data = animals)   
summary(re.out)
```
]

## Example: Palmer Penguins

.pull-left[
```{r eval=FALSE,fig.align="center",fig.width=6,fig.height=6}
# this package needs to be installed
library(palmerpenguins)

w  <- complete.cases(penguins)
df <- data.frame(penguins[w, c(1, 4, 3)])

ggplot(data = df,
       mapping = aes(x = bill_depth_mm, 
                     y = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(col = as.numeric(df$species)) +
  xlab("Bill Depth (mm)") + ylab("Bill Length (mm)")
```
]

.pull-right[
```{r echo=FALSE,fig.align="center",fig.width=6,fig.height=6}
# this package needs to be installed
library(palmerpenguins)

w  <- complete.cases(penguins)
df <- data.frame(penguins[w, c(1, 4, 3)])

ggplot(data = df, 
       mapping = aes(x = bill_depth_mm, 
                     y = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(col = as.numeric(df$species)) +
  xlab("Bill Depth (mm)") + ylab("Bill Length (mm)")
```
]


---

## Example: Palmer Penguins

.pull-left[
```{r}
# regress bill length upon bill depth
lm.out <- lm(bill_length_mm ~ bill_depth_mm, 
             data = df)
AIC(lm.out)
```
]

.pull-right[
```{r echo=FALSE,fig.align="center",fig.width=6,fig.height=6}
ggplot(data = df, mapping = aes(x = bill_depth_mm, y = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(col = as.numeric(df$species)) +
  geom_abline(slope = lm.out$coefficients[2], 
              intercept = lm.out$coefficients[1], col = "blue") +
  xlab("Bill Depth (mm)") + ylab("Bill Length (mm)")
```
]


---

## Example: Palmer Penguins - Random Intercepts

.pull-left[
```{r}
# regress bill length upon bill depth
#  with a random species effect (random intercepts)
lm.out <- lmer(bill_length_mm ~ bill_depth_mm + 
                 (1 | species), 
               data = df)
coef(lm.out)$species
AIC(lm.out)   
# much lower - a better model
```
]

.pull-right[
```{r echo=FALSE,fig.align="center",fig.width=6,fig.height=6}
cf <- coef(lm.out)$species
ggplot(data = df, mapping = aes(x = bill_depth_mm, y = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(col = as.numeric(df$species)) +
  geom_abline(slope = cf[1, 2], intercept = cf[1, 1], col = "black") +
  geom_abline(slope = cf[2, 2], intercept = cf[2, 1], col = "red") +
  geom_abline(slope = cf[3, 2], intercept = cf[3, 1], col = "green") +
  xlab("Bill Depth (mm)") + ylab("Bill Length (mm)")
```
]


---

## Example: Palmer Penguins - Random Slopes

.pull-left[
```{r}
# regress bill length upon bill depth
#  with a random species effect (random slopes)
lm.out <- lmer(bill_length_mm ~ bill_depth_mm + 
              (0 + bill_depth_mm | species), 
              data = df)
coef(lm.out)$species
AIC(lm.out) 
# still substantially lower - a better model still
```
]

.pull-right[
```{r echo=FALSE,fig.align="center",fig.width=6,fig.height=6}
cf <- coef(lm.out)$species
ggplot(data = df, mapping = aes(x = bill_depth_mm, y = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(col = as.numeric(df$species)) +
  geom_abline(slope = cf[1, 2], intercept = cf[1, 1], col = "black") +
  geom_abline(slope = cf[2, 2], intercept = cf[2, 1], col = "red") +
  geom_abline(slope = cf[3, 2], intercept = cf[3, 1], col = "green") +
  xlab("Bill Depth (mm)") + ylab("Bill Length (mm)")
```
]


---

## Example: Palmer Penguins - Random Intercepts and Slopes

.pull-left[
```{r message=FALSE}
# regress bill length upon bill depth
#  with a random species effect 
#  (both random intercepts and slopes)
lm.out <- lmer(bill_length_mm ~ bill_depth_mm + 
              (bill_depth_mm | species), 
              data = df)
coef(lm.out)$species
AIC(lm.out) 
# slightly higher than before - not the best model
```
]

.pull-right[
```{r echo=FALSE,fig.align="center",fig.width=6,fig.height=6}
cf <- coef(lm.out)$species
ggplot(data = df, mapping = aes(x = bill_depth_mm, y = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(col = as.numeric(df$species)) +
  geom_abline(slope = cf[1, 2], intercept = cf[1, 1], col = "black") +
  geom_abline(slope = cf[2, 2], intercept = cf[2, 1], col = "red") +
  geom_abline(slope = cf[3, 2], intercept = cf[3, 1], col = "green") +
  xlab("Bill Depth (mm)") + ylab("Bill Length (mm)")
```
]
